ent_method_zero_moment_point.name: Zero Moment Point
ent_method_zero_moment_point.summary: Foundational stability criterion for bipedal walking and balance control.
ent_method_zero_moment_point.body:
## Overview

The Zero Moment Point (ZMP) is a point on the ground where the horizontal moment components of the ground reaction force are zero. It is a core criterion for the dynamic balance of humanoid robots: if the ZMP lies within the support polygon, the robot theoretically will not tip over about the edge of the ground contact. The ZMP reduces the complex whole-body dynamic stability problem to a geometric criterion, making it the most widely used stability measure in gait planning and whole-body control.

ent_method_impedance_control.name: Impedance Control
ent_method_impedance_control.summary: A control approach that regulates the dynamic relationship between interaction force and displacement, making the robot behave like a virtual mechanical impedance.
ent_method_impedance_control.body:
## Overview

Impedance Control is a compliant control framework established by Hogan in 1985: rather than directly commanding position or force, it controls the **dynamic relationship** the robot presents to the environment—a virtual inertia-damping-stiffness ("spring-damper" behavior). Motion deviation serves as input, force as output, enabling the robot to exhibit designable compliance during contact. It is the underlying control semantics for safe interaction between humanoid robots and the environment/humans (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 14 §14.2.4; Hogan 1985, DOI 10.1115/1.3140702).

## Overview

OpenVLA is an open-source Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model and method recipe released in 2024 by Stanford and other institutions: a 7B-parameter Prismatic VLM backbone (Llama 2 + DINOv2/SigLIP dual vision encoders), pre-trained on approximately 970,000 real robot episodes from Open X-Embodiment, with actions generated autoregressively as discrete tokens. As a method, its value lies in establishing the de facto open-source VLA standard of "cross-embodiment pre-training + parameter-efficient fine-tuning + standardized evaluation" (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 19 §19.3.2; arXiv:2406.09246).

ent_method_system_identification.name: System Identification
ent_method_system_identification.summary: The process of building mathematical models of dynamical systems from measured input-output data, used to align simulation with reality.
ent_method_system_identification.body:
## Overview

System Identification is a methodological framework for estimating a robot's true dynamic parameters (mass, center of mass, inertia tensor, friction, actuator gains and delays) from experimental data. The core mathematical fact is that rigid-body dynamics equations are **linear** in these parameters—$\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}},\ddot{\mathbf{q}})\,\boldsymbol{\pi}$—so least squares can be used to solve for the base parameter set from torque-motion data. It is a common prerequisite for both the sim-to-real "gap reduction" pipeline and high-precision model-based control (MPC/WBC) (source: Project Wiki Chapter 8 §8.3.10, Chapter 18 §18.6.3).

## Overview

Domain Adaptation is a family of methods for adapting representations or policies learned in a source domain (typically simulation) to a target domain (the real world): fine-tuning the encoder with a small amount of target-domain data, learning a mapping between source-domain and target-domain observations, or aligning the feature distributions of the two domains. ent_method_gait_planning.name: Gait Planning
ent_method_gait_planning.summary: The generation of footstep sequences, timing, and phase transitions that produce stable and efficient locomotion for legged robots.
ent_method_gait_planning.body:
## Overview

Gait Planning generates step sequences and footholds for bipedal walking: under the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM), the Zero Moment Point (ZMP) criterion ensures dynamic balance, and the Capture Point (CP)/Divergent Component of Motion (DCM) transforms "will it fall" into a geometric problem of "where to step next." The classic implementation is ZMP preview control (Kajita 2003), while modern implementations are typically organized via MPC/WBC (Sources: Project Wiki Chapter 8 §8.4.4, §8.4.9; Kajita 2003, DOI 10.1109/ROBOT.2003.1241826).

ent_method_shooting_method.summary: A numerical method for solving boundary-value problems by integrating from an initial guess and adjusting decision variables to satisfy terminal constraints.
ent_method_shooting_method.body:
## Overview

The Shooting Method is a numerical technique for solving two-point Boundary Value Problems (BVPs). Its core idea is to transform the boundary value problem into an Initial Value Problem (IVP) through iterative solving. What it truly changes is not the choice of solver, but rather the conversion of the global constraint of "satisfying boundary conditions" into a local iterative process of "adjusting the initial guess," thereby making boundary value problems, which cannot be solved directly, tractable.

ent_method_admittance_control.name: Admittance Control
ent_method_admittance_control.summary: A control approach that converts measured external forces into desired position or velocity trajectories, complementary to impedance control.
ent_method_admittance_control.body:
## Overview

Admittance Control is the "dual" method of impedance control: it computes the desired motion trajectory based on measured contact forces, which is then tracked by a position/velocity controller. Its fundamental equation is \(\mathbf{M}_d (\ddot{\mathbf{x}}_d - \ddot{\mathbf{x}}_c) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}}_d - \dot{\mathbf{x}}_c) + \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x}_c) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\). What it truly changes is not the way force is controlled, but rather the transfer of the "force-motion" coupling relationship from the torque level to the trajectory level—allowing existing high-precision position control hardware to directly participate in compliant interaction.

ent_method_diffusion_policy.name: Diffusion Policy
ent_method_diffusion_policy.summary: A visuomotor policy that represents action distributions as denoising diffusion models, enabling multimodal and smooth robot action generation.
ent_method_diffusion_policy.body:
## Overview

Diffusion Policy is an imitation learning method proposed by Chi et al. in 2023: it models the conditional distribution of action chunks \(p(a_{t:t+k}\mid o_t)\) as a denoising diffusion process, iteratively generating a smooth sequence of actions starting from noise. Its core advantage is the **natural representation of multimodal action distributions** (facing demonstrations where "going left or right are both acceptable" does not result in learning a compromise), combined with receding-horizon execution to balance smoothness and closed-loop responsiveness. It has become the mainstream policy form for complex manipulation tasks (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 18 §18.4; arXiv:2303.04137).

ent_method_model_predictive_control.name: Model Predictive Control (MPC)
ent_method_model_predictive_control.summary: An optimization-based control method that repeatedly solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem using a predictive model and applies only the first control action.
ent_method_model_predictive_control.body:
## Overview

Model Predictive Control (MPC) solves a finite-horizon open-loop optimal control problem at each control cycle, but **only executes the first control step**, then re-solves with a new state estimate in the next cycle—this receding-horizon mechanism gives MPC both the foresight of optimization and the robustness of feedback. It is the primary optimization-based control framework for handling hard constraints (joint limits, torque saturation, friction cones, ZMP support polygons) in humanoid robots (source: Project Wiki Chapter 14 §14.4).

ent_method_domain_randomization.summary: A sim-to-real technique that randomizes simulation parameters during training to improve policy robustness against real-world model mismatch.
ent_method_domain_randomization.body:
## Overview

Domain Randomization (DR) is the most commonly used sim-to-real technique: during training, simulation parameters (mass, friction, damping, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, lighting, textures, latency, etc.) are randomized so that the policy performs well across a parameterized distribution family—the real world is just one sample from that distribution. It was systematically proposed by Tobin et al. in 2017 (visual randomization) and extended to dynamics randomization by Peng et al. in 2018, becoming the de facto standard for transferring reinforcement learning in legged and humanoid robots (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 18 §18.6.2; arXiv:1703.06907; arXiv:1710.06537).

## Overview

Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) is an imitation learning method proposed by Zhao et al. in 2023 on the low-cost dual-arm teleoperation platform ALOHA: instead of regressing single-step actions frame by frame, the policy predicts a sequence of future k actions at once, combined with a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to absorb demonstration style diversity and temporal ensembling to smooth outputs. It achieves 80%–90% success rates on fine-grained dual-arm tasks with approximately $20K-level hardware and around 50 demonstrations. "Action chunking" has become the mainstream design for action heads in robot foundation models (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 18 §18.3; arXiv:2304.13705).

ent_method_hierarchical_qp_wbc.body:
## Overview

Hierarchical QP Whole-Body Control (HQP WBC) is a strict-priority implementation of whole-body control: tasks such as "maintain balance > track end-effector trajectory > avoid joint limits" are ordered by priority, with higher-priority tasks fully satisfied before lower-priority tasks are solved only within their null space, each layer solving a QP or synthesized via null-space projection. It addresses the unacceptable issue in safety-critical scenarios where weighted-sum methods allow tasks to "compromise" with each other (source: project Wiki Chapter 8 §8.4.10.2; Escande et al. 2014, DOI 10.1177/0278364914521306).

ent_method_pid_control.name: PID Control
ent_method_pid_control.summary: A foundational feedback control method that computes a control signal as a linear combination of proportional, integral, and derivative terms of the tracking error.
ent_method_pid_control.body:
## Overview

PID control (Proportional-Integral-Derivative control) is the workhorse algorithm for joint servos: the proportional term provides immediate correction, the integral term eliminates steady-state error, and the derivative term provides damping to suppress overshoot. In humanoid robots, it operates in a **cascade structure**—the innermost current loop (i.e., torque loop, with bandwidth in the kilohertz range), the middle velocity loop, and the outermost position loop, with inner-loop bandwidth 3–10 times higher than the outer loop layer by layer. Between textbook PID and production-ready PID lie three engineering details: anti-windup, derivative filtering, and feedforward compensation (source: Project Wiki Chapter 14 §14.2).

## Overview

Action token prediction is an action representation method that discretizes continuous robot actions into discrete bins, maps them into the language model vocabulary, and thereby transforms action generation into a "next token prediction" problem. It was established by the RT series and inherited by open-source VLAs such as OpenVLA. Its greatest advantage is **full reuse of the LLM training and inference ecosystem**; the cost is quantization error, sequence length, and high-frequency jitter, which gave rise to two improvement routes: FAST frequency-domain compression and diffusion/flow-matching continuous action heads (Source: Project Wiki Chapter 19 §19.2.2).
